title: Space Nukes: A 60-Year Ban Nobody Can Enforce
summary:
For nearly 60 years, nuclear weapons have been banned from space, thanks to the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. Both the US and the Soviet Union agreed not to put weapons of mass destruction in orbit. But there's a glaring loophole: no one has ever had a reliable way to verify compliance. A warhead could be hidden inside an ordinary-looking satellite, and we'd never know until it's too late.

Now, MIT physicist Areg Danagoulian has proposed a solution. His idea involves a satellite-based sensor that uses high-energy protons trapped by Earth's magnetic field as a probe. When these protons interact with radioactive materials like uranium, they produce a burst of neutrons—a telltale signature. A detector about the size of an encyclopedia could identify these neutrons from up to 2.5 miles away after about a week of observation.

The stakes are high. A nuclear detonation in space could destroy thousands of satellites in a single blast, creating dangerous debris. The consequences were demonstrated in 1962 when the US conducted Starfish Prime, a 1.45-megaton explosion 250 miles above the Pacific. It knocked out radio communications, created artificial auroras, and damaged eight of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time. Radiation lingered for five years, and it even set off burglar alarms in Hawaii.

But detection is easier said than done. Getting close enough to inspect another satellite would require maintaining proximity, which could raise suspicions. "Satellite operators get really freaked out," said Thomas González Roberts of Georgia Tech. "If another satellite is spending too much time next to you, you might think that they're spying on you."

There's also the question of whether this is a solution in search of a problem. Deliberate nuclear attacks on satellites are rare because they're so destructive. "You're going to take out more than just that target," Roberts said, and any attacker would likely damage their own satellites too. As Brian Weeden of Aerospace Corp. put it, "The policy problems are always the bigger challenge than the technical problems." So while the science is promising, the real hurdles are diplomatic.
why_it_matters: Satellites now affect everyday life more than most people realize—weather forecasts, GPS, internet maps, financial transactions, and even school projects often depend on space-based systems. If a nuclear weapon in space could destroy thousands of satellites and create dangerous debris, then the inability to verify a 60-year-old ban is not just a military problem; it is a risk to the shared infrastructure that connects the planet.

It would photograph the inside of every satellite.

background_read: In 1962, the United States tested a nuclear weapon high above the Pacific in an operation called Starfish Prime; the blast knocked out radio communications and damaged satellites, giving governments an early warning of what space-based nuclear weapons could do.
Those dangers helped produce the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, in which the United States, the Soviet Union, and many other nations agreed not to place weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

The treaty has no real inspection mechanism, and satellites can be launched in secret or disguised as ordinary spacecraft, which is why the physicist Areg Danagoulian (a researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) is proposing a detector that looks for neutron bursts produced when radiation meets uranium.

As the article notes, even this kind of science faces practical objections: Thomas González Roberts (a security researcher at Georgia Tech, a major U.S. technology university) points out that satellite operators would distrust any spacecraft that lingered too close to them.

Brian Weeden, who works at Aerospace Corp. (a nonprofit organization that analyzes space security), argues that the toughest barrier is not technical but diplomatic—agreeing on what counts as verification and how much mutual inspection nations will accept.

perspectives.description: Danagoulian's proposed sensor could give the Outer Space Treaty a credible, non-invasive way to check for hidden warheads without opening another country's satellite. If the science works, the ban would become more meaningful and harder to break secretly.

A satellite designed to inspect other spacecraft can look like a weapon or a spy, so the technology itself might increase distrust in orbit. A false positive—mistaking normal materials for uranium—could also become an excuse for confrontation between major powers.

The history of arms control often follows the same pattern: a dramatic event such as Starfish Prime inspires a treaty, but the treaty is only as strong as its verification. Technical proposals are necessary, yet they cannot solve the underlying problem of whether states are willing to trust one another.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking / the future of space rules
perspectives.description: If this kind of detector is ever deployed, governments will still need to negotiate how close one nation's satellite may get to another's and what counts as allowed inspection. Those decisions could set precedents for how outer space is governed in the coming age of commercial satellites, space stations, and even space mining.
